name: Battle of the Yarmuk
info: In August 636 the Rashidun Caliphate's army under Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated a larger Byzantine army under Vahan near the Yarmuk River, which ended Byzantine rule in Syria and opened the way to Egypt.

facts.date: 15 to 20 August 636, six days of fighting; some accounts say the battle lasted a day
facts.place: The plain east of Wadi-ur-Ruqqad, south-east of the Golan Heights and east of the Sea of Galilee, near the Yarmuk River on what is now the border between Syria and Jordan
facts.sides: The Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Ubayda, who handed command to Khalid ibn al-Walid, with 36,000 to 40,000 men in most early accounts; the Byzantine Empire under the field commander Vahan, with 60,000 to 70,000 in most early accounts, though modern estimates run from 15,000 to 20,000 up to 80,000 to 100,000 or more
facts.outcome: The Byzantine army was routed on the sixth day. Khalid then entered Damascus, and Heraclius withdrew to Constantinople and left Syria.

t: Khalid withdrew the Muslim forces from Syria and gathered them on the Yarmuk plain, which forced the Byzantines to bring their five armies together too, in a battle Heraclius had wished to avoid.
For five days Khalid fought mainly on the defensive, using a mounted reserve to counter each Byzantine attack; on the sixth he massed about 8,000 cavalry and drove the Byzantine horse from the field.

Estimates of the armies differ widely: most early accounts put the Byzantines at 60,000 to 70,000 and the Muslims at 36,000 to 40,000, while some modern estimates for the Byzantine army are as low as 15,000 to 20,000.
dyk: Early Muslim sources say Gregory's Byzantine infantry were chained together in lengths of ten men as a sign that they would not retreat; modern historians suggest instead that they used the Graeco-Roman testudo formation.
ev: Heraclius wins at Nineveh, and Khosrow II is overthrown soon after
Muhammad dies, Abu Bakr becomes caliph and puts down the Ridda revolts
Abu Bakr calls for the invasion of Syria, and the Byzantines are beaten at Ajnadayn
Muslim forces take Emesa, and Heraclius prepares a counterattack
Heraclius launches his offensive and the Byzantine army gathers at Antioch
Six days of fighting at the Yarmuk end with the rout of the Byzantine army
Amr ibn al-As invades and conquers Byzantine Egypt

sections.background:
Heraclius became emperor in 610, during the Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628. The Sasanians overran Syria in 611 and went on to conquer Palestine and Egypt. Heraclius launched his offensive in 622 and won a victory at Nineveh in 627. Khosrow II was then overthrown and killed in a coup led by his son Kavad II, who sued for peace and agreed to withdraw from all occupied Byzantine territory. In 629 Heraclius restored the True Cross to Jerusalem.

Meanwhile Muhammad had preached Islam in Arabia and by 630 had brought most of it under a single political authority. After his death in June 632 Abu Bakr was chosen caliph and defeated rebel tribes in the Ridda Wars of 632–633. He then began wars of conquest, first in Iraq under Khalid ibn al-Walid, and in February 634 issued a call to arms for the invasion of Syria. The Byzantines were beaten at Ajnadayn in July, Damascus fell in September, and the last significant garrison of Palestine was routed at Fahl.

Abu Bakr's successor Umar wished to carry the conquest deeper into Syria. He replaced Khalid with Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah. Tiberias and Baalbek fell without much struggle, and Emesa early in 636. Heraclius, alarmed, prepared to win back the lost regions. In 635 Yazdegerd III of Persia sought an alliance and was to attack in Iraq at the same time, but he could not coordinate with Heraclius's offensive of May 636, probably because his government was exhausted.
sections.forces:
By May 636 Heraclius had gathered a large force at Antioch, with contingents of Slavs, Franks, Georgians, Armenians, Christian Arabs, Lombards, Avars, Khazars, Balkans and Göktürks, organised in five armies. Theodore Trithyrius was their joint leader and Vahan, an Armenian and former garrison commander of Emesa, was overall field commander, with an Armenian army. Qanatir, a Slavic prince, led the Slavs, Jabalah ibn al-Aiham, king of the Ghassanid Arabs, a Christian Arab force, and Gregory and Dairjan the remaining contingents. Heraclius supervised from Antioch and did not wish to fight one pitched battle. He planned to attack the divided Muslim corps one by one.

The Muslims learned of this from Byzantine prisoners. On Khalid's advice Abu Ubayda gathered the whole army in one place, and after raids and the risk of an attack on the rear it moved to the eastern plain of the Yarmuk. In a council of war Abu Ubayda gave command to Khalid, who formed 36 infantry regiments and four cavalry regiments and kept his elite mobile guard in reserve. The line was 12 kilometres long and faced west. The Byzantine line, about 13 kilometres long and facing east, had gaps between its divisions, and its heavy cavalry stood behind the infantry.

Most early accounts give the Muslims 36,000 to 40,000 and the Byzantines 60,000 to 70,000. Some modern estimates put the Byzantine army at 40,000 at most, others at 15,000 to 20,000, and the Rashidun army at 15,000 to 40,000, most likely around 36,000. Warren Treadgold suggests 80,000 to 100,000 or more for the Byzantines, while acknowledging the uncertainty.
sections.course:
Both armies were in position in late July, and for about a month there was only a skirmish and talks. The fighting began on 15 August. Champions from each side duelled, and Vahan sent a third of his infantry in a limited attack at midday, which lacked determination. Muslim chronicles record that George, a Byzantine unit commander, rode over to the Muslim line, became a Muslim and died fighting on that side the same day. On 16 August Vahan attacked at dawn, hoping to catch the Muslims at morning prayers, but Khalid had set outposts. Qanatir's Slavs pushed back the Muslim right and Yazid's left wing was driven back to its camps, but Khalid's mobile guard restored both flanks. Muslim women in the camps, led by Hind, are said to have turned the retreating men back, and Dairjan was killed.

On 17 and 18 August Vahan pressed the Muslim right and right centre, which fell back twice and were rallied, and each time Khalid struck the Byzantine flanks with his mobile guard. On the fourth day Byzantine horse archers wounded many Muslims in the eyes, so that it became known as the Day of Lost Eyes. Ikrimah's 400 cavalry covered the Muslim retreat, and all were killed or badly wounded. Ikrimah died that evening.

On 19 August Vahan asked for a truce, and Khalid refused. He massed about 8,000 horsemen and sent Dhirar with 500 cavalry by night to take the bridge at Ayn Dhakar. On 20 August the Muslim cavalry rode round the Byzantine left, routed the Byzantine horse to the north, and attacked the infantry from the rear. The Byzantines fell back west towards the ravine of Wadi-ur-Ruqqad, where Dhirar already held the bridge. Some fell into the ravines or were killed in flight, and many escaped.
sections.aftermath:
Theodore Trithyrius was killed on the field. Niketas escaped to Emesa, and Jabalah escaped, briefly came to terms with the Muslims and then went back to the Byzantine court. The Muslims took no prisoners in the battle but may have captured some in the pursuit. Khalid and his mobile guard went north after the survivors, found them near Damascus and attacked. Vahan, who had escaped the field, was probably killed there. Khalid then entered Damascus, where the residents welcomed him.

When the news reached Heraclius at Antioch he was devastated and enraged. He blamed his own wrongdoings, above all his marriage to his niece Martina. He no longer had the men or the money to defend the province. He held a service of intercession in the cathedral of Antioch, where his advisers told him almost unanimously, and he accepted, that the defeat was God's decision and the result of the sins of the people of the land, himself among them. He then sailed by night to Constantinople. Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem, is said to have secretly put the True Cross and other relics on a ship to protect them from the Arabs.

Heraclius turned to the defence of Anatolia and Egypt. Byzantine Armenia fell to the Muslims in 638–639, and he created a buffer zone in central Anatolia by ordering all the forts east of Tarsus to be evacuated. In 639–642 Amr ibn al-As, who had commanded the Muslim right at the Yarmuk, invaded and captured Byzantine Egypt.
sections.sources:
Most early accounts are Arab, and they generally agree that the Byzantines and their allies outnumbered the Muslims two to one. The only early Byzantine source is Theophanes, who wrote a century later. Accounts disagree on the length of the battle, some giving a day and others six. Several details come from Muslim chronicles and tradition: George's conversion, the verse sung by the women, Heraclius's farewell to Syria, and the chains of Gregory's infantry, which modern historians read instead as a testudo. Greek court sources accused Vahan of treason for disobeying Heraclius's order to avoid a large battle.

The size of the armies is the main dispute. One estimate of the Byzantine army, 60,000 to 70,000, was reached by considering the supply and the weakened state of the empire after 628, while Treadgold argues from the empire's fiscal capacity and pay records for far more. Other scholars point to logistical limits and give no figure.
sections.legacy:
The battle ended Byzantine rule in Syria and was the culmination of the first great wave of early Muslim conquests after Muhammad's death, which carried the Rashidun Caliphate into both the Sasanian and Byzantine empires. It is regarded as one of the most decisive battles in military history. It was Khalid ibn al-Walid's greatest victory and made his reputation as a tactician and cavalry commander.

Assessments of the Byzantine side stress its failures. Its commanders let the enemy choose the field, held their cavalry in static reserve for most of the six days, and never concentrated their numbers for a breakthrough, even when they gained one on the fourth day. The lack of resolve may have come from the difficulty of commanding an army divided by internal conflict, and Vahan's numbers may have been of little use in the terrain. Khalid, in this reading, carried out on the field on a small scale what Heraclius had planned on a grand scale, defeating a larger force in parts by moving quickly.

George F. Nafziger, in Islam at War, calls the Yarmuk one of the most decisive battles in human history and argues that a Byzantine victory would have left the modern world unrecognisable.

summary: In August 636 Khalid ibn al-Walid's Muslim army fought six days at the Yarmuk against a Byzantine army that most early accounts put at about twice its size, and on the last day routed it. Syria was lost to Heraclius, and Egypt fell within six years.

notes: Sources section is short because the article says little of its sources; it is mostly the disputes.

The article's numbers: 36,000 to 40,000 vs 60,000 to 70,000 in early accounts; 'two to one' also from Arab sources. Modern estimates are given in a loose way (Byzantine 40,000 at most, or 15,000 to 20,000; Rashidun 15,000 to 40,000, most likely 36,000).
Article says Heraclius 'incestuous marriage to his niece Martina'; I wrote 'marriage to his niece'.

Left out as likely vandalised or garbled: 'Jabalah ibn al-Ayham' spelled differently from 'al-Aiham'; 'Jarajis' among rivals of Vahan (a name given once with no other mention); Heraclius's 'fear of water' and pontoon bridge; the quoted farewell to Syria; the women's song; Day 1 outposts; the dead commander 'wrapped in a cloak'.

Article contradicts itself on Amr: right wing commander in the Muslim line but described as a corps commander in Palestine earlier; and on Qanatir's Slavs, said both to be the Byzantine left wing and to hold the Muslim right wing (day 3).
Early sentences: 'Khalid was replaced by Abu Ubayda' vs a later account in which Abu Ubayda hands command to Khalid in a council of war; both are given.
Article's lead says 'decisive Arab victory'; I used 'decisive' only as the article does, attributed to regard and Nafziger.
Day-of-Lost-Eyes and Abu Sufyan's lost eye are tradition; Abu Sufyan left out. The Muslim reinforcements of 6,000 under Umar and the Companions present were left out for length.
